{{Short description|Exact solution to the Einstein field equations}}
{{use mdy dates|date=June 2024}}
{{general relativity|expanded=solutions}}
In [[general relativity]], the '''Oppenheimer–Snyder model''' is a solution to the [[Einstein field equations]] based on the [[Schwarzschild metric]] describing the collapse of an object of extreme mass into a [[black hole]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite book 
|last1=McEvoy |first1=J. P. 
|title=Introducing Stephen Hawking 
|last2=Zarate |first2=Oscar 
|publisher=Totem Books 
|year=1995 |isbn=978-1-874-16625-2}}</ref> It is named after physicists [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]] and [[Hartland Snyder]], who published it in 1939.<ref name=":4" />

During the collapse of a star to a black hole the geometry on the outside of the sphere is the Schwarzschild geometry. However the geometry inside is the same [[Robertson-Walker coordinates|Robertson-Walker geometry]] as in the rest of the observable universe.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hamilton |first=Andrew |date=November 13, 2011 |title=Collapse to a Black Hole |url=https://jila.colorado.edu/~ajsh/bh/collapse.html |access-date=February 29, 2024 |website=JILA, University of Colorado, Boulder}}</ref>

== History ==
[[Albert Einstein]], who had developed his theory of [[general relativity]] in 1915, initially denied the possibility of black holes,<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal |last=Bernstein |first=Jeremy |title=The Reluctant Father of Black Holes |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-reluctant-father-of-black-holes-2007-04/ |access-date=2023-08-03 |journal=[[Scientific American]] |date=2007 |volume=17 |pages=4–11 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0407-4sp |language=en|url-access=subscription }}</ref> even though they were a genuine implication of the Schwarzschild metric, obtained by [[Karl Schwarzschild]] in 1916, the first known non-trivial exact solution to Einstein's field equations.<ref name=":2" /> In 1939, Einstein published "On a Stationary System with Spherical Symmetry Consisting of Many Gravitating Masses" in the ''[[Annals of Mathematics]]'', claiming to provide "a clear understanding as to why these '[[Gravitational singularity|Schwarzschild singularities]]' do not exist in physical reality."<ref name=":02" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Isaacson |first=Walter |title=Einstein: His Life and Universe |title-link=Einstein: His Life and Universe |publisher=[[Simon & Schuster]] |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-7432-6473-0 |location=New York |pages= |chapter=Chapter Eleven: Einstein's Universe}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=250-1}}

Months after the issuing of Einstein's article,<ref name=":02" /> [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]] and his student [[Hartland Snyder]] studied this topic with their paper "On Continued Gravitational Contraction" making the opposite argument as Einstein's.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Oppenheimer |first1=J.R. |last2=Snyder |first2=H. |author-link2=Hartland Snyder |year=1939 |title=On Continued Gravitational Contraction |journal=[[Physical Review]] |volume=56 |issue=5 |pages=455–459 |bibcode=1939PhRv...56..455O |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.56.455 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":7" />{{Reference page|pages=250-1}} They showed when a sufficiently massive star runs out of thermonuclear fuel, it will undergo continued gravitational contraction and become separated from the rest of the universe by a boundary called the [[event horizon]], which not even light can escape. This paper predicted the existence of what are today known as black holes.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last1=Pais |first1=Abraham |author-link=Abraham Pais |title=J. Robert Oppenheimer: A Life |last2=Crease |first2=Robert |author-link2=Robert P. Crease |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-195-32712-0 |pages=}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=31-2}} The term "black hole" was coined decades later, in the fall of 1967, by [[John Archibald Wheeler]] at a conference held by the [[Goddard Institute for Space Studies]] in New York City;<ref name=":6" />{{Reference page|pages=31-2}} it appeared for the first time in print the following year.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Bartusiak |first=Marcia |title=Black Hole: How an Idea Abandoned by Newtonians, Hated by Einstein, and Gambled on by Hawking Became Loved |publisher=[[Yale University Press]] |year=2015 |isbn=978-0-300-21085-9 |location=New Haven, CT |chapter=Chapter 9: Why Don't You Call It A Black Hole? |author-link=Marcia Bartusiak}}</ref> In this paper, Oppenheimer and Snyder used Einstein's own theory of gravity to prove how black holes could develop for the first time in contemporary physics, but without referencing the aforementioned article by Einstein.<ref name=":02" /> Oppenheimer and Snyder did, however, refer to an earlier article by Oppenheimer and [[Robert Serber]] on [[neutron star]]s,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Oppenheimer |first1=J.R. |last2=Serber |first2=Robert |author-link2=Robert Serber |year=1938 |title=On the Stability of Stellar Neutron Cores |journal=[[Physical Review]] |volume=54 |issue=7 |pages=540 |bibcode=1938PhRv...54..540O |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.54.540}}</ref> improving upon the work of [[Lev Landau|Lev Davidovich Landau]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Landau |first=Lev D. |date=1938 |title=Origin of Stellar Energy |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/141333b0 |journal=Nature |volume=141 |pages=333–334 |doi=10.1038/141333b0|url-access=subscription }}</ref> in what was essentially an exercise in nuclear physics and gravitation.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=269}} 

This investigation attracted the attention of [[Richard C. Tolman|Richard Chace Tolman]], who had previously obtained an exact solution to the Einstein field equations describing a [[Static spherically symmetric perfect fluid|static ideal fluid sphere]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tolman |first=Richard C. |date=1939 |title=Static Solutions of Einstein's Field Equations for Spheres of Fluid |url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.55.364 |journal=Physical Review |volume=55 |issue=364 |pages=364–373 |bibcode=1939PhRv...55..364T |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.55.364 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Oppenheimer and [[George Volkoff]] subsequently published paper on the stability of neutron stars,  the [[Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit|Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Oppenheimer |first=J. Robert |last2=Volkoff |first2=George |date=1939 |title=On Massive Neutron Cores |url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.55.374 |journal=Physical Review |volume=55 |issue=374 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.55.374}}</ref> These papers established the foundation for the general-relativistic theory of stellar structure.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=269}} Actually, the objects Tolman, Oppenheimer, and Volkoff studied were the neutron stars of [[Fritz Zwicky]] rather than the "neutron cores" of Lev Landau. But while Zwicky did introduce the notion of neutron stars, much of his work on this topic was later rejected as wrong. By contrast, the paper by Oppenheimer and Volkoff has been accepted as correct.<ref name=":9">{{Cite book |last=Thorne |first=Kip |author-link=Kip Thorne |title=Black Holes and Time Warps: Einstein's Outrageous Legacy |title-link=Black Holes and Time Warps |publisher=W. W. Norton & Company |year=1994 |isbn=0-393-03505-0 |location=New York}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=206-7}} This led Oppenheimer to consider the natural next problem of determining what would happen if a neutron star were so heavy it would collapse due to its own weight.<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|pages=211-2}}

However, Oppenheimer would not revisit the topic in future publications.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=McGrath |first=Jenny |title='Oppenheimer' fact v. fiction: A nuclear historian breaks down what the movie got right and wrong |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/oppenheimer-fact-vs-fiction-what-the-movie-got-right-wrong-2023-7 |access-date=2023-08-02 |website=[[Business Insider]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Model ==
The Oppenheimer–Snyder model of continued [[gravitational collapse]] is described by the line element<ref name="physicsforums">{{cite web 
|last1=Donis |first1=Peter 
|title=Oppenheimer-Snyder Model of Gravitational Collapse: Mathematical Details 
|url=https://www.physicsforums.com/insights/oppenheimer-snyder-model-of-gravitational-collapse-mathematical-details/ 
|website=Physics Forums Insights |access-date=3 October 2023 |date=9 January 2023}}</ref><math display="block">
ds^2 = -d\tau^2 + A^2(\eta) \left(\frac{dR^2}{1 - 2M \frac{R^2_-}{R^2_b} \frac{1}{R_+}} + R^2 \, d\Omega^2 \right)
</math>The quantities appearing in this expression are as follows:
* The coordinates are <math>(\tau, R, \theta, \phi)</math> where <math>\theta, \phi</math> are [[Spherical coordinate system|spherical coordinates]].
* <math>R_b > 0</math> is the boundary of the matter region
* <math>M > 0</math> the mass.
* <math>R_- = \mathrm{min}(R, R_b)</math> and <math>R_+ = \mathrm{max}(R, R_b)</math>.
* <math>\eta</math> is defined [[Implicit function|implicitly]] by the equation
<math display = block> \tau(\eta, R) = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt \frac{R_+^3}{2M} (\eta + \sin \eta).</math>
* <math>A(\eta) = \frac{1 + \cos \eta}{2}</math>.

This expression is valid both in the matter region <math>R < R_b</math>, and the vacuum region <math>R > R_b</math>, and continuously transitions between the two.

== Reception and legacy ==
[[Kip Thorne]] recalled that physicists were initially skeptical of the model, viewing it as "truly strange" at the time.<ref name=":0" /> He explained further, "It was hard for people of that era to understand the paper because the things that were being smoked out of the mathematics were so different from any mental picture of how things should behave in the universe."<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last1=Bird |first1=Kai |author-link=Kai Bird |title=American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer |title-link=American Prometheus |last2=Sherwin |first2=Martin J. |author-link2=Martin J. Sherwin |publisher=Vintage Books |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-375-72626-2 |location=New York |pages=}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=89-90}} [[Werner Israel]] noted that the work of Oppenheimer and his collaborators on the end states of [[Compact object|compact objects]] had actually been foreshadowed by the discovery of [[Chandrasekhar limit|an upper limit]] on the mass of a [[white dwarf]] by [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]]. Yet, like the works of Oppenheimer and his colleagues, this was initially rejected and almost forgotten.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last=Israel |first=Werner |date=2000 |title=Black Hole 2000: The Astrophysical Era |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1086/316557 |journal=Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific |volume=112 |issue=772 |pages=583-585 |doi=10.1086/316557}}</ref> While physicists had become used to the relativity of the passage of time in different frames of reference, the [[gravitational time dilation]] implied by the Oppenheimer-Snyder model was too extreme for most physicists at the time to accept. For a distant inertial observer, the surface of the star undergoing continued gravitational implosion would freeze at the critical radius (the Schwarzschild radius) but for an observer on the surface of the star, the process would continue. Moreover, any light emitted at the critical radius would be infinitely red shifted, making the star appear to "cut itself off" from the external universe.<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|pages=214-8}}

Oppenheimer himself thought little of this discovery.<ref name=":4" /> However, some considered the model's discovery to be more significant than Oppenheimer did,<ref name=":4" /> and the model would later be described as forward thinking.<ref name=":0" /> [[Freeman Dyson]] thought it was Oppenheimer's greatest contribution to science. Lev Davidovich Landau added the Oppenheimer-Snyder paper to his "golden list" of classic papers.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Bartusiak |first=Marcia |title=Black Hole: How an Idea Abandoned by Newtonians, Hated by Einstein, and Gambled on by Hawking Became Loved |publisher=[[Yale University Press]] |year=2015 |isbn=978-0-300-21085-9 |location=New Haven, CT |chapter=Chapter 6: Only Its Gravitational Field Persists |author-link=Marcia Bartusiak}}</ref> Due to Landau's influence, most Soviet theoretical physicists accepted this result as well.<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|page=219}} [[John Archibald Wheeler]] was initially an opponent of the model until the late 1950s,<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" /> when he was asked to teach a course on general relativity at Princeton University.<ref name=":3" /> Wheeler claimed at a conference in 1958 that the Oppenheimer-Snyder model had neglected the many features of a realistic star.<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|pages=209-11}} Indeed, in order to keep the mathematics manageable, Oppenheimer and Snyder assumed a perfectly spherical star with no spin, zero internal pressure, uniform density, no mass ejection, no [[shock wave]]s, and no radiation emission.<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|pages=216-7}} However, he later changed his mind completely after being informed by [[Edward Teller]] of the results of a [[computer simulation]] ran by [[Stirling Colgate]] and his team at the [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]].<ref name=":2" /> Colgate and his colleagues adapted the computer codes for developing the thermonuclear bomb (the [[History of the Teller–Ulam design|Teller-Ulam design]]) to simulate the gravitational implosion of a star. They assumed that the star was spherical and not rotating, but otherwise took into account all the complications of a real star. They found that a sufficiently heavy star would undergo continued gravitational contraction in a manner similar to the idealized scenario described by Oppenheimer and Snyder.<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|pages=238-9}} Independently, a team led by [[Yakov Borisovich Zeldovich]] relied on their own expertise and computer simulations for the Soviet Union's hydrogen bomb (the [[Sakharov's Third Idea|Sakharov-Zeldovich idea]]) and reached the same conclusion.<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|pages=240-1}}
[[File:Chandra Image of Sgr A* with Labels (2003-0203long-more-1).tiff|thumb|Labeled image of Sagittarius A* taken by the Chandra X-ray Observatory in 2003]]
At  the First [[Texas Symposium on Relativistic Astrophysics]] in 1963, Wheeler gave a lengthy lecture on gravitational contraction, in which he shared his enthusiasm for the Oppenheimer-Snyder model.<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|page=240}} He  subsequently played a key role in reviving interest in general relativity in the United States, and popularized the term "black hole" in the late 1960s.<ref name=":3" /> Various theoretical physicists pursued this topic<ref name=":7" />{{Reference page|pages=250-1}} and by the late 1960s and early 1970s, advances in observational astronomy, such as [[radio telescope]]s, changed the attitude of the scientific community.<ref name=":5" />{{Reference page|pages=89-90}} [[Pulsar]]s and [[Quasar|quasars]] had already been discovered and neither neutron stars nor black holes were considered mere textbook curiosities.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last=Pais|first=Abraham|title=Subtle Is the Lord: The Science and the Life of Albert Einstein|title-link=Subtle is the Lord|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2005|isbn=978-0-192-80672-7|pages=|chapter=Chapter 15: The New Dynamics|orig-date=1982|author-link=Abraham Pais}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=269}}<ref name=":10" /> [[Cygnus X-1]], the first solid black-hole candidate, was discovered by the ''[[Uhuru (satellite)|Uhuru]]'' X-ray space telescope in 1971.<ref name=":2" /> Observations of the central radio source of the Milky Way, [[Sagittarius A*]], and the center of the spiral galaxy [[Messier 106|NGC 4258]], both of which identified as [[supermassive black hole]]s, came in the 1990s.<ref name=":10" /> Further evidence arrived in the 2000s thanks to the [[Hubble Space Telescope]] and the [[Chandra X-ray Observatory]]. The works of Oppenheimer and his collaborates was the initial impetus for this golden age of astrophysics.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cassidy|first=David|author-link=David C. Cassidy|title=A Short History of Physics in the American Century|publisher=Harvard University Press|year=2011|isbn=978-0-674-04936-9|location=Cambridge, MA}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=165-6}} [[Jeremy Bernstein]] described the Oppenheimer-Snyder publication as "one of the great papers in twentieth-century physics."<ref name=":5" />{{Reference page|pages=89-90}}

A mental block for many physicists who were skeptical of the Oppenheimer-Snyder model was the so-called "Schwarzschild singularity"—meaning the boundary of a black hole—which turned out to be a removable by a change of coordinates. (The central singularity, however, cannot be removed.) In 1958, [[David Finkelstein]] found such [[Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates|a coordinate transformation]] and gave a lecture on it at [[King's College London]]. [[Roger Penrose]] was in attendance. ([[Arthur Eddington|Arthur Stanley Eddington]] had introduced the same idea earlier, but the true significance of this insight was not understood and it was soon forgotten.)<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|pages=244-51}} Penrose won the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] in 2020 for his contributions to the mathematical theory of black holes, one of the frontiers of modern theoretical physics.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Blum |first=Alexander |last2=Bonolis |first2=Luisa |last3=Lalli |first3=Roberto |last4=Gomez |first4=Juan-Andres Leon |last5=Renn |first5=Jürgen |author-link5=Jürgen Renn |date=December 8, 2020 |title=From the Renaissance of Einstein's General Theory of Relativity to the Confirmation of the Black Hole Paradigm |url=https://www.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/feature-story/renaissance-einsteins-general-theory-relativity-confirmation-black-hole-paradigm |department=Feature Story |publisher=Max Planck Society for the History of Science}}</ref> He credited the Oppenheimer–Snyder model as one of his inspirations for research.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nobel Prize Foundation |date=March 2021 |title=Roger Penrose Interview |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2020/penrose/interview/ |access-date=August 5, 2023 |website=The Nobel Prize}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

''[[The Hindu]]'' wrote in 2023:<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |date=2023-07-29 |title=Oppenheimer: Remembering the physics that first made him great |language=en-IN |work=[[The Hindu]] |url=https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/science/oppenheimer-snyder-stellar-collapse-black-hole-formation/article67131932.ece |access-date=2023-08-02 |issn=0971-751X}}</ref>
{{Blockquote|text=The world of physics does indeed remember the paper. While Oppenheimer is remembered in history as the “father of the atomic bomb”, his greatest contribution as a physicist was on the physics of black holes. The work of Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder helped transform black holes from figments of mathematics to real, physical possibilities – something to be found in the cosmos out there.}}

== In popular culture ==

* In the 2023 film [[Oppenheimer (film)|''Oppenheimer'']], an interaction between Oppenheimer and his student Snyder occurs as their paper was published on the same day as the [[invasion of Poland]].<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Nate |date=2023-07-25 |title=What's Fact and What's Fiction in Oppenheimer? |url=https://www.vulture.com/2023/07/oppenheimer-historical-accuracy-what-really-happened.html |access-date=2023-08-02 |website=[[Vulture (website)|Vulture]] |language=en-us}}</ref>
